questions.sentence: She ___ in Madrid since 2019.
questions.explanation: Use the present perfect with "since" + a point in time for situations that started in the past and continue now.

questions.sentence: I ___ my keys. I can't get into the house!
questions.explanation: The present perfect shows a past action with a result now (I still don't have my keys).

questions.sentence: We ___ to Paris three times so far.
questions.explanation: "So far" means "up to now", so we use the present perfect for experiences.

questions.sentence: I ___ him yesterday at the station.
questions.explanation: "Yesterday" is a finished time, so we use the past simple, not the present perfect.

questions.sentence: Have you ___ been to Japan?
questions.explanation: "Ever" is used in present perfect questions about experiences in someone's whole life.

questions.sentence: I haven't finished my homework ___.
questions.explanation: "Yet" goes at the end of negative sentences and questions in the present perfect.

questions.sentence: Don't worry, I've ___ booked the tickets.
questions.explanation: "Already" shows something happened sooner than expected. It usually goes between "have" and the past participle.

questions.sentence: They ___ for the bus for forty minutes and it still hasn't come.
questions.explanation: The present perfect continuous emphasises the duration of an activity that is still happening.

questions.sentence: Your eyes are red. Have you ___?
questions.explanation: The present perfect continuous explains present evidence of a recent activity.

questions.sentence: This is the best film I have ___ seen.
questions.explanation: After a superlative, we often use "ever" with the present perfect: the best ... I have ever seen.

questions.sentence: It's the first time I ___ sushi.
questions.explanation: After "It's the first time...", English uses the present perfect.

questions.sentence: How long ___ each other?
questions.explanation: "Know" is a state verb, so we use the present perfect simple (not continuous) to talk about duration.

questions.sentence: I've worked here ___ six months.
questions.explanation: Use "for" with a period of time (six months) and "since" with a starting point (since May).

questions.sentence: I've been learning English ___ I was eight.
questions.explanation: "Since" introduces the starting point of a situation that continues now.

questions.sentence: She ___ three books this year, and she's writing a fourth.
questions.explanation: Use the present perfect simple to say how many things have been completed.

questions.sentence: I ___ on this report all morning, and I'm exhausted.
questions.explanation: The present perfect continuous focuses on a long, continuous activity that explains how you feel now.

questions.sentence: My brother has ___ to Canada. He'll be back next month.
questions.explanation: "Has gone to" means he is still there; "has been to" means he went and came back.

questions.sentence: Have you ever ___ to Australia?
questions.explanation: For completed experiences (go and come back), use "been to".

questions.sentence: I ___ my best friend since we were five.
questions.explanation: "Know" is a state verb, so we use the present perfect simple with "since".

questions.sentence: We ___ a lot of rain recently.
questions.explanation: "Recently" with a situation connected to now takes the present perfect.

questions.sentence: She's ___ left. You've just missed her!
questions.explanation: "Just" means a very short time ago and goes between "have" and the past participle.

questions.sentence: This exam was ___ than the last one.
questions.explanation: Two-syllable adjectives ending in -y change to -ier in the comparative.

questions.sentence: Mount Everest is the ___ mountain in the world.
questions.explanation: Short adjectives form the superlative with "the" + -est.

questions.sentence: My new phone is ___ expensive than my old one.
questions.explanation: Long adjectives form the comparative with "more".

questions.sentence: She's the ___ person I've ever met.
questions.explanation: Long adjectives form the superlative with "the most".

questions.sentence: Today is ___ than yesterday.
questions.explanation: "Bad" is irregular: bad, worse, the worst.

questions.sentence: He's ___ footballer in the team.
questions.explanation: "Good" is irregular: good, better, the best.

questions.sentence: The weather is getting ___.
questions.explanation: We repeat the comparative to show a continuous change: colder and colder.

questions.sentence: The more you practise, ___ you'll become.
questions.explanation: The structure is "the + comparative ..., the + comparative ...".

questions.sentence: This book isn't ___ interesting as the film.
questions.explanation: "Not as + adjective + as" means "less ... than".

questions.sentence: My sister is ___ taller than me.
questions.explanation: Use "much", "far" or "a lot" before a comparative to show a big difference.

questions.sentence: The test was ___ more difficult than I expected.
questions.explanation: "Far" can modify a comparative to mean "much".

questions.sentence: Of all the students, Lucia works ___.
questions.explanation: "Hard" as an adverb has a regular superlative: the hardest.

questions.sentence: This sofa is ___ comfortable as the old one.
questions.explanation: "Just as + adjective + as" means "exactly equal".

questions.sentence: Could you drive a bit ___? I'm feeling sick.
questions.explanation: For adverbs ending in -ly, use "more" to form the comparative.

questions.sentence: Which is the ___ city in your country?
questions.explanation: Long adjectives and past participles form the superlative with "the most".

questions.sentence: He's ___ older than his wife: only two months.
questions.explanation: "Slightly" or "a bit" before a comparative shows a small difference.

questions.sentence: This is by ___ the best restaurant in town.
questions.explanation: "By far" emphasises a superlative.

questions.sentence: London is ___ from Madrid than Paris is.
questions.explanation: "Far" has the comparative "further" (or "farther").

questions.sentence: The film was ___ than I thought it would be.
questions.explanation: Long adjectives (including -ing adjectives) use "more" in the comparative.

questions.sentence: My grandmother is the ___ member of our family.
questions.explanation: Short adjectives take -est in the superlative.

questions.sentence: Your essay is ___ than mine, but mine is more creative.
questions.explanation: Two-syllable adjectives ending in -y take -ier.

questions.sentence: I enjoy ___ in the mountains at the weekend.
questions.explanation: "Enjoy" is always followed by a gerund (-ing).

questions.sentence: She decided ___ a personal trainer.
questions.explanation: "Decide" is followed by the infinitive with "to".

questions.sentence: He gave up ___ two years ago.
questions.explanation: After a phrasal verb like "give up", use the gerund.

questions.sentence: I can't afford ___ a gym membership right now.
questions.explanation: "Afford" is followed by the infinitive with "to".

questions.sentence: ___ regularly is good for your heart.
questions.explanation: A gerund can be the subject of a sentence.

questions.sentence: I'm looking forward to ___ you next week.
questions.explanation: In "look forward to", "to" is a preposition, so it is followed by the gerund.

questions.sentence: Remember ___ the lights when you leave.
questions.explanation: "Remember + infinitive" means remember to do something you need to do in the future.

questions.sentence: I remember ___ this song when I was a child.
questions.explanation: "Remember + -ing" means you have a memory of something in the past.

questions.sentence: He stopped ___ a drink because he was thirsty.
questions.explanation: "Stop + infinitive" means stop one activity in order to do another.

questions.sentence: You should stop ___ so much sugar. It's bad for you.
questions.explanation: "Stop + -ing" means you no longer do that activity.

questions.sentence: She's really good at ___ tennis.
questions.explanation: After a preposition (at), use the gerund.

questions.sentence: My doctor advised me ___ more water.
questions.explanation: "Advise someone to do something": use the infinitive after the object.

questions.sentence: I tried ___ the window, but it was stuck.
questions.explanation: "Try + infinitive" means make an effort to do something difficult.

questions.sentence: If you have a headache, try ___ a glass of water.
questions.explanation: "Try + -ing" means do something as an experiment to see if it helps.

questions.sentence: They let us ___ early yesterday.
questions.explanation: "Let" is followed by object + base form (no "to").

questions.sentence: I'm not used to ___ up so early.
questions.explanation: In "be used to", "to" is a preposition, so it is followed by the gerund.

questions.sentence: It's important ___ before you exercise.
questions.explanation: After "It's + adjective", use the infinitive with "to".

questions.sentence: Would you mind ___ the door?
questions.explanation: "Mind" is followed by the gerund.

questions.sentence: She refused ___ the medicine.
questions.explanation: "Refuse" is followed by the infinitive with "to".

questions.sentence: I went to the gym ___ fit.
questions.explanation: Use the infinitive of purpose to explain why you do something.

questions.sentence: He admitted ___ the last biscuit.
questions.explanation: "Admit" is followed by the gerund.

questions.sentence: ___ it was raining, we went for a run.
questions.explanation: "Although" is followed by a full clause (subject + verb).

questions.sentence: ___ the rain, we went for a run.
questions.explanation: "Despite" is followed by a noun or noun phrase, not a clause.

questions.sentence: In spite ___ his injury, he finished the race.
questions.explanation: The complete expression is "in spite of" + noun/-ing.

questions.sentence: The gym is expensive. ___, the classes are excellent.
questions.explanation: "However" connects two sentences and is followed by a comma.

questions.sentence: My brother loves team sports, ___ I prefer swimming alone.
questions.explanation: "Whereas" compares two contrasting facts within one sentence.

questions.sentence: ___ feeling tired, she went to her yoga class.
questions.explanation: "Despite" can be followed by the -ing form of a verb.

questions.sentence: ___ though he trains every day, he isn't very fit.
questions.explanation: "Even though" is a stronger form of "although".

questions.sentence: Running is good for your heart. ___, it can be hard on your knees.
questions.explanation: "On the other hand" introduces a contrasting point at the start of a sentence.

questions.sentence: Despite the fact ___ it was cold, they swam in the sea.
questions.explanation: "Despite the fact that" + clause is correct; "despite" alone needs a noun.

questions.sentence: ___ some people prefer to exercise in the morning, others prefer the evening.
questions.explanation: "While" can be used like "whereas" to contrast two ideas.

questions.sentence: She eats very healthily. Her husband, ___, lives on junk food.
questions.explanation: "On the other hand" can go in the middle of a sentence between commas.

questions.sentence: The diet was hard to follow. It worked, ___.
questions.explanation: "Though" can go at the end of a sentence in informal English to mean "however".

questions.sentence: ___ having little time, he cooks fresh food every day.
questions.explanation: "In spite of" is followed by a noun or -ing form.

questions.sentence: I like cycling. ___, my sister prefers running.
questions.explanation: "In contrast" starts a new sentence to show a difference.

questions.sentence: ___ my friends love the gym, I find it boring.
questions.explanation: "Although" + clause can begin a sentence.

questions.sentence: He's very strong, ___ he isn't very fast.
questions.explanation: "But" joins two contrasting clauses in one sentence.

questions.sentence: ___ being older, my grandfather is fitter than me.
questions.explanation: "Despite + -ing" shows a contrast.

questions.sentence: Some sports are expensive. Running, ___, costs almost nothing.
questions.explanation: "However" can appear in the middle of a sentence between commas.

questions.sentence: Swimming is a low-impact sport, ___ running puts pressure on your joints.
questions.explanation: "Whereas" connects two contrasting facts in one sentence.

questions.sentence: ___ all our efforts, we lost the match.
questions.explanation: "Despite" + noun phrase (all our efforts).

questions.sentence: I know it's healthy. ___, I can't stand broccoli!
questions.explanation: "Even so" means "despite what was just said" and starts a sentence.

questions.sentence: The letter ___ yesterday.
questions.explanation: Past simple passive: was/were + past participle.

questions.sentence: English ___ all over the world.
questions.explanation: Present simple passive: am/is/are + past participle.

questions.sentence: The new bridge ___ at the moment.
questions.explanation: Present continuous passive: am/is/are + being + past participle.

questions.sentence: The results ___ next week.
questions.explanation: Future passive: will be + past participle.

questions.sentence: Three people ___ in the accident.
questions.explanation: We use the passive when the action is more important than who did it.

questions.sentence: The thief ___ by the police last night.
questions.explanation: Use "by" to say who did the action in a passive sentence.

questions.sentence: My phone ___. I can't find it anywhere!
questions.explanation: Present perfect passive: has/have been + past participle.

questions.sentence: The room ___ before the guests arrive.
questions.explanation: Modal passive: modal + be + past participle.

questions.sentence: The emails ___ when I got to the office.
questions.explanation: Past perfect passive: had been + past participle.

questions.sentence: It ___ that social media affects our mood.
questions.explanation: "It is said that..." is an impersonal passive used to report general opinions.

questions.sentence: He is ___ to be the richest man in the country.
questions.explanation: "He is believed to be..." is a passive reporting structure.

questions.sentence: The house ___ while we were on holiday.
questions.explanation: Past continuous passive: was/were + being + past participle.

questions.sentence: This photo ___ by my grandfather in 1965.
questions.explanation: "Take" is irregular: take, took, taken.

questions.sentence: Messages ___ every day on social media.
questions.explanation: Present simple passive for regular, general actions.

questions.sentence: The meeting has ___ until Friday.
questions.explanation: Present perfect passive: has been + past participle.

questions.sentence: Children shouldn't ___ alone near the pool.
questions.explanation: Modal passive: should (not) + be + past participle.

questions.sentence: Was the window ___ by the wind?
questions.explanation: Passive questions: was/were + subject + past participle.

questions.sentence: The film is going to ___ in cinemas next month.
questions.explanation: "Going to" passive: going to be + past participle.

questions.sentence: Our family friend ___ an award for his charity work.
questions.explanation: Verbs with two objects can have a person as the passive subject: He was given an award.

questions.sentence: It ___ that friendships are less sincere online.
questions.explanation: "It has been suggested that..." is a hedging structure used in formal writing.

questions.sentence: The invitations ___ printed yet.
questions.explanation: Negative present perfect passive: haven't been + past participle.

topics.title: Used to, be used to, get used to

questions.sentence: When I was a child, I ___ climb trees every day.
questions.explanation: "Used to + base form" describes past habits that don't happen anymore.

questions.sentence: I ___ living in a big city now. It doesn't bother me.
questions.explanation: "Be used to + -ing" means something is familiar and normal for you.

questions.sentence: It took me months to ___ driving on the left.
questions.explanation: "Get used to + -ing" describes the process of something becoming familiar.

questions.sentence: Did you ___ have long hair?
questions.explanation: In questions and negatives with "did", we write "use to" (without -d).

questions.sentence: She ___ like coffee, but now she drinks it every day.
questions.explanation: Negative past habit: didn't use to + base form.

questions.sentence: I'm not used to ___ so early.
questions.explanation: After "be used to", use the -ing form.

questions.sentence: My parents are slowly ___ used to their new house.
questions.explanation: "Get used to" can be used in continuous tenses to show the process is happening.

questions.sentence: We ___ live in Seoul, but we moved to Madrid in 2018.
questions.explanation: "Used to" describes a past situation that is no longer true.

questions.sentence: He's a nurse, so he ___ working at night.
questions.explanation: "Be used to" describes something familiar because you do it often.

questions.sentence: You'll soon ___ the noise of the traffic.
questions.explanation: "Get used to + noun" means become familiar with it.

questions.sentence: There ___ be a cinema here, but now it's a supermarket.
questions.explanation: "There used to be" describes something that existed in the past.

questions.sentence: I ___ eating spicy food when I lived in Mexico.
questions.explanation: "Got used to + -ing" shows that something became familiar over time.

questions.sentence: Where did you ___ go on holiday as a child?
questions.explanation: After "did" in questions, use "use to".

questions.sentence: I can't ___ to this cold weather.
questions.explanation: "Can't get used to" means you are unable to become comfortable with something.

questions.sentence: She ___ speaking in public; she does it every week.
questions.explanation: "Be used to + -ing" = it is normal for her.

questions.sentence: My grandfather ___ walk five kilometres to school.
questions.explanation: "Used to + base form" for repeated actions in the past.

questions.sentence: Living alone was strange at first, but I'm ___ used to it.
questions.explanation: "I'm getting used to it" shows the process is still happening.

questions.sentence: Were you ___ to the heat when you lived in Spain?
questions.explanation: "Were you used to + noun/-ing?" asks if something was familiar to you.

questions.sentence: I never ___ to enjoy reading, but now I love it.
questions.explanation: "Never used to + base form" is another way to make the negative.

questions.sentence: New employees take time to ___ used to the system.
questions.explanation: After "to" (infinitive), use "get used to".

questions.sentence: I ___ to working from home now, so going back to the office will be hard.
questions.explanation: "Have got used to" shows the process is complete.

questions.sentence: If it ___ tomorrow, we'll stay at home.
questions.explanation: First conditional: If + present simple, will + base form.

questions.sentence: If I ___ more money, I would buy a new laptop.
questions.explanation: Second conditional: If + past simple, would + base form (imaginary situation).

questions.sentence: If you study hard, you ___ the exam.
questions.explanation: First conditional result: will + base form for a likely future result.

questions.sentence: If I ___ you, I would talk to your teacher.
questions.explanation: In the second conditional, "If I were you" is the standard form for advice.

questions.sentence: I ___ a scholarship if my grades were better.
questions.explanation: Second conditional result: would + base form.

questions.sentence: ___ you finish your dissertation on time, you won't graduate this year.
questions.explanation: "Unless" means "if ... not".

questions.sentence: What would you do if you ___ the lottery?
questions.explanation: Second conditional for imaginary situations: If + past simple.

questions.sentence: If she ___ the bus, she'll be late for class.
questions.explanation: First conditional: If + present simple.

questions.sentence: We'll go to the beach ___ the weather is good.
questions.explanation: "If" introduces a real possibility in the first conditional.

questions.sentence: If I lived near the university, I ___ walk to class.
questions.explanation: "Could" can replace "would" in the second conditional to express possibility.

questions.sentence: If he ___ harder, he would get better marks.
questions.explanation: Second conditional: If + past simple for something that is not true now.

questions.sentence: You can borrow my notes ___ you give them back tomorrow.
questions.explanation: "As long as" means "only if".

questions.sentence: If I ___ the answer, I'd tell you.
questions.explanation: Second conditional: the speaker doesn't know the answer now.

questions.sentence: If you ___ your homework, you can go out.
questions.explanation: "If + present simple" with "can" for permission in a real situation.

questions.sentence: I'll call you as soon as I ___ home.
questions.explanation: After time expressions like "as soon as", use the present simple for the future.

questions.sentence: If they ___ the course, they will get a certificate.
questions.explanation: First conditional: present simple in the if-clause.

questions.sentence: If I ___ to a different university, would I be happier?
questions.explanation: Second conditional question for an imaginary situation.

questions.sentence: If you don't hurry, you ___ the lecture.
questions.explanation: First conditional with a negative if-clause.

questions.sentence: She would travel more if she ___ so busy.
questions.explanation: Second conditional: "if + past simple (weren't)" for an unreal present situation.

questions.sentence: If the school ___ more money, it could build a new library.
questions.explanation: Second conditional: If + past simple, could/would + base form.

questions.sentence: Take an umbrella ___ it rains.
questions.explanation: "In case" means "as a precaution because something might happen".

questions.sentence: You ___ see a doctor about that cough.
questions.explanation: "Should + base form" is the most common way to give advice.

questions.sentence: You ___ to revise more before the exam.
questions.explanation: "Ought to + base form" means the same as "should".

questions.sentence: You'd better ___ now or you'll miss the train.
questions.explanation: "Had better + base form (no to)" gives strong advice or a warning.

questions.sentence: If I ___ you, I'd apply for that scholarship.
questions.explanation: "If I were you, I'd..." is a common way to give advice.

questions.sentence: You ___ better not be late again.
questions.explanation: The negative is "had better not + base form".

questions.sentence: Why ___ you ask your teacher for help?
questions.explanation: "Why don't you...?" is a friendly way to make a suggestion.

questions.sentence: I suggest ___ a study group.
questions.explanation: "Suggest" is followed by the -ing form (or "that + clause").

questions.sentence: It's a good idea ___ breaks while studying.
questions.explanation: "It's a good idea + infinitive" is used to give advice.

questions.sentence: You shouldn't ___ so late; you need your sleep.
questions.explanation: "Shouldn't + base form" gives negative advice.

questions.sentence: I recommend ___ notes during the lecture.
questions.explanation: "Recommend" can be followed by the -ing form.

questions.sentence: My teacher recommended that I ___ more English films.
questions.explanation: "Recommend that + subject + base form" is a formal structure.

questions.sentence: What do you think I ___ do?
questions.explanation: Use "should" in questions to ask for advice.

questions.sentence: You ought not ___ your phone during exams.
questions.explanation: The negative is "ought not to + base form".

questions.sentence: How ___ asking your parents for advice?
questions.explanation: "How about + -ing?" makes a suggestion.

questions.sentence: You ___ really try to get more exercise.
questions.explanation: "Should" can be made stronger with "really".

questions.sentence: If I were in your position, I ___ the job offer.
questions.explanation: Second conditional structure used to give advice.

questions.sentence: She advised me ___ the first answer that came into my head.
questions.explanation: "Advise someone not to do something" is the negative pattern.

questions.sentence: You'd better ___ tell anyone about this.
questions.explanation: "Had better not + base form".

questions.sentence: It might be worth ___ to a careers advisor.
questions.explanation: "It's worth + -ing" means it would be useful to do it.

questions.sentence: Have you ___ about starting your essay earlier?
questions.explanation: "Have you thought about + -ing?" is a polite suggestion.

questions.sentence: I think you ___ to apologise to her.
questions.explanation: Only "ought" is followed by "to" here.

questions.sentence: Can you give me some ___ about hotels in Buenos Aires?
questions.explanation: "Information" is uncountable: it has no plural and no "a/an".

questions.sentence: We don't have ___ time before our flight.
questions.explanation: Use "much" with uncountable nouns like "time".

questions.sentence: How ___ suitcases are you taking?
questions.explanation: Use "many" with plural countable nouns.

questions.sentence: I need ___ advice about travelling in South America.
questions.explanation: "Advice" is uncountable, so use "some", not "a/an".

questions.sentence: There's ___ luggage in the hall. Whose is it?
questions.explanation: "Luggage" is uncountable, so use "a lot of" or "much".

questions.sentence: She bought ___ new furniture for her flat.
questions.explanation: "Furniture" is uncountable.

questions.sentence: I've got ___ friends in Seoul, so I won't be lonely.
questions.explanation: "A few" is used with plural countable nouns and means "some".

questions.sentence: There's ___ milk left. Can you buy some more?
questions.explanation: "Little" is used with uncountable nouns and means "not much".

questions.sentence: The ___ were very helpful at the tourist office.
questions.explanation: "Staff" is a group noun and normally takes no -s.

questions.sentence: We had ___ terrible weather on our holiday.
questions.explanation: "Weather" is uncountable, so we say "such terrible weather" (no "a").

questions.sentence: Could I have ___ of bread, please?
questions.explanation: Use a unit expression like "a slice of" to count uncountable nouns.

questions.sentence: The ___ in this city is awful at rush hour.
questions.explanation: "Traffic" is uncountable.

questions.sentence: How ___ money did you spend in Paris?
questions.explanation: "Money" is uncountable, so use "how much".

questions.sentence: There were too ___ people at the airport.
questions.explanation: "People" is a plural countable noun, so use "many".

questions.sentence: I'm afraid there is ___ evidence to support that claim.
questions.explanation: "Evidence" is uncountable; "little" means "not enough".

questions.sentence: We've made good ___ with our plans.
questions.explanation: "Progress" is uncountable.

questions.sentence: My ___ have arrived but my suitcase hasn't.
questions.explanation: "Bag" is countable; "luggage" and "baggage" are uncountable.

questions.sentence: I'd like ___ glass of water, please.
questions.explanation: "Glass" is countable here (a container), so use "a".

questions.sentence: There aren't ___ hostels in this village.
questions.explanation: Use "any" in negative sentences.

questions.sentence: I have ___ homework tonight.
questions.explanation: "Homework" is uncountable.

questions.sentence: He gave me ___ useful piece of advice.
questions.explanation: "A piece of advice" makes the uncountable noun countable.

questions.sentence: I'd love to visit ___ Andes one day.
questions.explanation: Use "the" with mountain ranges.

questions.sentence: She's ___ engineer.
questions.explanation: Use "an" before a vowel sound.

questions.sentence: ___ Mount Everest is in Nepal.
questions.explanation: We don't use an article with single mountains.

questions.sentence: We stayed in a hotel near the beach. ___ hotel was lovely.
questions.explanation: Use "the" when the listener already knows which one (it was mentioned before).

questions.sentence: He plays ___ guitar in a band.
questions.explanation: Use "the" with musical instruments after "play".

questions.sentence: I go to ___ school by bus.
questions.explanation: We don't use "the" with "school" when we talk about its main purpose.

questions.sentence: ___ Amazon is the largest rainforest in the world.
questions.explanation: Use "the" with rivers and the names of rainforests.

questions.sentence: It's ___ honour to meet you.
questions.explanation: "Honour" starts with a vowel sound (the h is silent), so use "an".

questions.sentence: She's studying at ___ university in Madrid.
questions.explanation: "University" starts with a /j/ sound, so use "a".

questions.sentence: ___ life is too short to be unhappy.
questions.explanation: No article with uncountable nouns used in a general sense.

questions.sentence: We had ___ lunch at a lovely café.
questions.explanation: No article before meals in general.

questions.sentence: ___ rich should pay more taxes.
questions.explanation: "The + adjective" refers to a group of people (the rich, the poor).

questions.sentence: I love ___ dogs, but I'm allergic to them.
questions.explanation: No article with plural nouns used in a general sense.

questions.sentence: Have you ever been to ___ United States?
questions.explanation: Use "the" with country names that include "States", "Kingdom" or "Republic".

questions.sentence: She's ___ best student in the class.
questions.explanation: Use "the" with superlatives.

questions.sentence: We travelled across ___ Atlantic by boat.
questions.explanation: Use "the" with oceans and seas.

questions.sentence: ___ Spain is famous for its food.
questions.explanation: Most country names don't take an article.

questions.sentence: I'll see you in ___ hour.
questions.explanation: "Hour" begins with a vowel sound (silent h).

questions.sentence: ___ moon looks huge tonight.
questions.explanation: Use "the" with things that are unique, like the moon, the sun and the sky.

questions.sentence: He's ___ only person who knows the truth.
questions.explanation: Use "the" with "only".

questions.sentence: What ___ amazing view!
questions.explanation: "What + a/an + adjective + singular noun" for exclamations.

questions.sentence: When I arrived at the cinema, the film ___.
questions.explanation: Past perfect: an action that happened before another past action.

questions.sentence: I ___ a book when the lights went out.
questions.explanation: Past continuous for an action in progress interrupted by another action.

questions.sentence: She ___ for two hours when she finally found the answer.
questions.explanation: Past perfect continuous: an activity in progress up to a point in the past.

questions.sentence: We ___ dinner, then we went for a walk.
questions.explanation: Past simple for completed actions in sequence.

questions.sentence: By the time the police arrived, the thief ___.
questions.explanation: "By the time" + past simple often goes with the past perfect.

questions.sentence: He was tired because he ___ all day.

questions.sentence: "We're watching the news," they said. → They said they ___ the news.
questions.explanation: Present continuous changes to past continuous.

questions.sentence: "I've finished the article," she said. → She said she ___ the article.
questions.explanation: Present perfect changes to past perfect.

questions.sentence: "I saw the film yesterday," he said. → He said he had seen the film ___.
questions.explanation: "Yesterday" changes to "the day before" or "the previous day".

questions.sentence: "Where do you live?" she asked. → She asked me where ___.
questions.explanation: Reported questions use statement word order (subject + verb), without "do/did".

questions.sentence: "Are you a journalist?" he asked. → He asked me ___ a journalist.
questions.explanation: Yes/no questions are reported with "if" or "whether".

questions.sentence: "I can't come," Ana said. → Ana said she ___ come.
questions.explanation: "Can" changes to "could".

questions.sentence: "I'll see you tomorrow," he said. → He said he'd see me ___.
questions.explanation: "Tomorrow" changes to "the next day" or "the following day".

questions.sentence: "Don't touch the screen," the teacher told us. → The teacher told us ___ the screen.
questions.explanation: Reported orders: tell someone (not) to do something.

questions.sentence: "Please sit down," she said to me. → She asked me ___ down.
questions.explanation: Reported requests: ask someone to do something.

questions.sentence: "What time does the show start?" he asked. → He asked what time the show ___.
questions.explanation: Reported question with statement word order and backshift.

questions.sentence: "I'm working here now," she said. → She said she was working ___.
questions.explanation: "Here" often changes to "there" in reported speech.

questions.sentence: "I was reading," he said. → He said he ___ reading.
questions.explanation: Past continuous can change to past perfect continuous.

questions.sentence: "We must leave," they said. → They said they ___ leave.
questions.explanation: "Must" (obligation) often changes to "had to".

questions.sentence: She told ___ the news was fake.
questions.explanation: "Tell" needs a person as its object: tell someone that...

questions.sentence: He said ___ the story was true.
questions.explanation: "Say" doesn't need a person; if you include one, use "say to someone".

questions.sentence: "Have you seen my phone?" she asked. → She asked if I ___ her phone.
questions.explanation: Present perfect in a question becomes past perfect.

questions.sentence: "This programme is excellent," he said. → He said that ___ programme was excellent.
questions.explanation: "This" often changes to "that" in reported speech.

questions.sentence: "I'm going to post it online," she said. → She said she ___ post it online.
questions.explanation: "Am/is going to" changes to "was going to".

questions.sentence: "Why are you laughing?" he asked. → He asked me why ___.
questions.explanation: Reported wh- questions: statement word order and backshift.

questions.sentence: "It wasn't me who broke it." → He denied ___ it.
questions.explanation: "Deny" is followed by the -ing form.

questions.sentence: "I'll help you with the article." → She offered ___ me with the article.
questions.explanation: "Offer" is followed by the infinitive.

questions.sentence: "You should check your sources." → The editor advised me ___ my sources.
questions.explanation: "Advise someone to do something".

questions.sentence: "I'm not going to apologise." → The politician refused ___.
questions.explanation: "Refuse + infinitive".

questions.sentence: "I'm sorry I was late." → He apologised ___ late.
questions.explanation: "Apologise for + -ing".

questions.sentence: "Would you like to come to the premiere?" → She invited me ___ to the premiere.
questions.explanation: "Invite someone to do something".

questions.sentence: "I'll definitely be there." → He promised ___ there.
questions.explanation: "Promise + infinitive".

questions.sentence: "Why don't we watch a documentary?" → She suggested ___ a documentary.
questions.explanation: "Suggest + -ing" (or "suggest that we watch").

questions.sentence: "You copied my homework!" → She accused him ___ her homework.
questions.explanation: "Accuse someone of + -ing".

questions.sentence: "Remember to post the letter." → He reminded me ___ the letter.
questions.explanation: "Remind someone to do something".

questions.sentence: "Yes, I took the money." → She admitted ___ the money.
questions.explanation: "Admit + -ing".

questions.sentence: "If you don't stop, I'll call the police!" → He threatened ___ the police.
questions.explanation: "Threaten + infinitive".

questions.sentence: "Don't go into the water!" → The lifeguard warned us ___ into the water.
questions.explanation: "Warn someone not to do something".

questions.sentence: "Well done for winning the prize!" → They congratulated her ___ the prize.
questions.explanation: "Congratulate someone on + -ing".

questions.sentence: "OK, I'll write the review." → He agreed ___ the review.
questions.explanation: "Agree + infinitive".

questions.sentence: "You should really try the new app." → She recommended ___ the new app.
questions.explanation: "Recommend + -ing".

questions.sentence: "Let's meet at 6." → He ___ meeting at 6.
questions.explanation: "Suggest + -ing" is used for proposals.

questions.sentence: "I didn't post that comment!" → She ___ posting the comment.
questions.explanation: "Deny + -ing" means say you didn't do something.

questions.sentence: "Please, please let me go to the concert!" → He begged his parents ___ him go.
questions.explanation: "Beg someone to do something".

questions.sentence: "Don't forget your passport." → Mum reminded me ___ my passport.
questions.explanation: "Remind someone not to do something".

questions.sentence: "I'm going to win this time." → She ___ that she would win.
questions.explanation: "Claim that + clause" means say something is true.

questions.sentence: You ___ wear a seatbelt in a car. It's the law.
questions.explanation: "Have to" expresses an obligation, often from a rule or law.

questions.sentence: You ___ take photos in the museum. It's forbidden.
questions.explanation: "Mustn't" means it is not allowed.

questions.sentence: You ___ bring food. Lunch is provided.
questions.explanation: "Don't have to" means it isn't necessary (but it isn't forbidden).

questions.sentence: Students ___ to use their phones during the exam.
questions.explanation: "Be (not) allowed to" talks about permission.

questions.sentence: ___ I leave early today? I have a dentist's appointment.
questions.explanation: "Can I...?" asks for permission.

questions.sentence: Guests are ___ to wear traditional clothes at the wedding.
questions.explanation: "Be supposed to" means it's expected (by rules or tradition).

questions.sentence: We ___ to queue for two hours to get into the festival.
questions.explanation: "Had to" is the past of "have to" and "must".

questions.sentence: You ___ tell her about the party. It's a surprise!
questions.explanation: "Mustn't" for something that is prohibited or a bad idea.

questions.sentence: My parents ___ me stay out until midnight on Saturdays.
questions.explanation: "Let someone do something" (no "to").

questions.sentence: Visitors are not ___ to feed the animals.
questions.explanation: "Be permitted to" is a formal way to talk about permission.

questions.sentence: You ___ worry. Everything is under control.
questions.explanation: "Needn't" means it's not necessary.

questions.sentence: I ___ to wear a uniform when I worked at the hotel.
questions.explanation: Past obligation: "had to".

questions.sentence: At my school, we ___ wear what we like on Fridays.
questions.explanation: "Can" for permission.

questions.sentence: Do we ___ to bring a present?
questions.explanation: "Do we have to...?" asks about obligation.

questions.sentence: You're ___ to arrive 30 minutes before the ceremony starts.
questions.explanation: "Be supposed to" for expectations.

questions.sentence: Children under 12 ___ enter without an adult.
questions.explanation: "Can't" for something not permitted.

questions.sentence: I ___ finish this report today. My boss says it's urgent.
questions.explanation: "Must" for strong personal or urgent obligation.

questions.sentence: Were you ___ to go to concerts when you were 14?
questions.explanation: "Were you allowed to...?" asks about past permission.

questions.sentence: You ___ show your ticket at the entrance, or they won't let you in.
questions.explanation: "Must" for an obligation.

questions.sentence: She ___ to take a day off for the festival. Her boss said yes.
questions.explanation: "Was allowed to" for permission in the past.

questions.sentence: They ___ us bring our own drinks to the event.
questions.explanation: "Don't let someone do something" = not allow.

questions.sentence: I ___ swim when I was four.
questions.explanation: "Could" for general ability in the past.

questions.sentence: After hours of trying, we ___ to find the hotel.
questions.explanation: "Manage to" for a specific success that was difficult.

questions.sentence: Despite the rain, they ___ finish the race.
questions.explanation: For a single achievement in the past, use "was/were able to" (not "could").

questions.sentence: I'd love to ___ play the guitar.
questions.explanation: "Can" has no infinitive, so use "be able to" after "love to".

questions.sentence: She ___ speak four languages.
questions.explanation: "Can + base form" for present ability.

questions.sentence: We succeeded ___ getting tickets for the festival.
questions.explanation: "Succeed in + -ing".

questions.sentence: He's good ___ dancing.
questions.explanation: "Good at + -ing/noun" describes ability.

questions.sentence: I ___ understand the instructions. They were in Chinese.
questions.explanation: "Couldn't" for inability in the past.

questions.sentence: Will you ___ come to the celebration on Friday?
questions.explanation: "Will be able to" for future ability (there is no "will can").

questions.sentence: I haven't ___ to contact her yet.
questions.explanation: "Have been able to" for ability in the present perfect.

questions.sentence: She's very ___ at organising events.
questions.explanation: "Skilled at" describes someone's ability.

questions.sentence: They didn't ___ to finish the decorations in time.
questions.explanation: "Didn't manage to" for failure to achieve something.

questions.sentence: He's ___ of running a marathon.
questions.explanation: "Capable of + -ing" describes ability.

questions.sentence: Sorry, I ___ hear you. The music is too loud.
questions.explanation: "Can't" for present inability.

questions.sentence: By next year, I ___ to drive.
questions.explanation: Future ability: "will be able to".

questions.sentence: I ___ never been able to whistle.
questions.explanation: "Have never been able to" for lifelong inability.

questions.sentence: She ___ to open the jar on her own.
questions.explanation: "Managed to" for a difficult achievement.

questions.sentence: My grandmother ___ read without glasses until she was 80.
questions.explanation: "Could" for general past ability over a period.

questions.sentence: I'm hopeless ___ cooking.
questions.explanation: "Hopeless at" for lack of ability.

questions.sentence: If you practise, you ___ be able to dance like a pro.
questions.explanation: First conditional: you will be able to.

questions.sentence: Were you ___ to see the fireworks from your window?
questions.explanation: "Were you able to...?" asks about ability on a specific occasion.

questions.sentence: She works ___ a shop assistant in Milan.
questions.explanation: "As" describes a job or role (she really is a shop assistant).

questions.sentence: He sings ___ a professional.
questions.explanation: "Like" means "similar to" (he isn't a professional).

questions.sentence: ___ I told you, the sale starts on Monday.
questions.explanation: "As" + clause means "in the same way that" in formal English.

questions.sentence: I used my coat ___ a pillow.
questions.explanation: "As" describes the function something has.

questions.sentence: This jacket looks ___ leather, but it's plastic.
questions.explanation: "Look like + noun" = similar in appearance.

questions.sentence: She's dressed ___ she's going to a wedding.
questions.explanation: "As if" + clause describes how something seems.

questions.sentence: Shops ___ Zara and Mango are very popular.
questions.explanation: "Like" or "such as" introduces examples.

questions.sentence: He's famous ___ a fashion designer.
questions.explanation: "Famous as" refers to someone's real role.

questions.sentence: The silk feels ___ water on your skin.
questions.explanation: "Feel like + noun" for comparison.

questions.sentence: Do it exactly ___ I showed you.
questions.explanation: "As" + clause, especially in formal English.

questions.sentence: ___ a customer, I expect good service.
questions.explanation: "As" = in the role of.

questions.sentence: It smells ___ fresh bread in here.
questions.explanation: "Smell like + noun".

questions.sentence: She treats her phone ___ a baby.
questions.explanation: "Like" = in a similar way to (it isn't really a baby).

questions.sentence: The shop is the same ___ it was ten years ago.
questions.explanation: "The same as" is a fixed comparison.

questions.sentence: Nobody sells shoes ___ these anymore.
questions.explanation: "Like these" = similar to these.

questions.sentence: He was employed ___ a security guard at the mall.
questions.explanation: "As" describes his job.

questions.sentence: It looks ___ it's going to rain.
questions.explanation: "Look as if" + clause.

questions.sentence: ___ most teenagers, she loves shopping online.
questions.explanation: "Like" = similar to.

questions.sentence: You can use this bag ___ a backpack too.
questions.explanation: "As" describes a function.

questions.sentence: She's very good at bargaining, just ___ her mother.
questions.explanation: "Just like" + noun = in the same way as.

questions.sentence: The market was ___ busy as usual.
questions.explanation: "As + adjective + as" for comparisons.

questions.sentence: I failed the test. I ___ studied harder.
questions.explanation: "Should have + past participle" expresses regret or criticism about the past.

questions.sentence: You ___ bought milk. We already had some in the fridge.
questions.explanation: "Needn't have + past participle": you did it, but it wasn't necessary.

questions.sentence: I ___ to wake up early, so I stayed in bed until 10.
questions.explanation: "Didn't need to + base form": it wasn't necessary, so you didn't do it.

questions.sentence: He ___ spent so much money on clothes. Now he can't pay his rent.
questions.explanation: "Shouldn't have" criticises a past action.

questions.sentence: We ___ to pay for the tickets. They were free.
questions.explanation: "Didn't have to" = it wasn't necessary.

questions.sentence: You ___ told me it was your birthday! I would have bought you a present.
questions.explanation: "Should have" for regret that something didn't happen.

questions.sentence: I ___ taken a taxi. The shop was only five minutes away.
questions.explanation: You did take a taxi, but it was unnecessary.

questions.sentence: She ___ to queue because she had a VIP ticket.
questions.explanation: She didn't queue because it wasn't necessary.

questions.sentence: They ___ left the shop without paying! That's stealing!
questions.explanation: Criticism of a past action: "shouldn't have".

questions.sentence: I ___ have worried. The interview went really well.
questions.explanation: "Needn't have worried" = I worried, but it was unnecessary.

questions.sentence: Did you ___ to show your ID at the shop?
questions.explanation: "Did you have to...?" asks about past obligation.

questions.sentence: We ___ booked a table. The restaurant was empty.
questions.explanation: Unnecessary action that was done: "needn't have".

questions.sentence: You ___ have bought that dress. It doesn't suit you.
questions.explanation: "Shouldn't have" for a bad decision.

questions.sentence: I ___ to buy a new phone because mine was repaired for free.
questions.explanation: "Didn't have to": no obligation, so I didn't buy one.

questions.sentence: He ___ have checked the price before he ordered.
questions.explanation: "Should have + past participle" for advice about the past.

questions.sentence: You ___ have brought an umbrella. It didn't rain at all.
questions.explanation: Unnecessary action: "needn't have".

questions.sentence: I ___ have listened to the shop assistant. The jacket was too small.
questions.explanation: Regret about following bad advice.

questions.sentence: We ___ to cook because Grandma brought dinner.
questions.explanation: "Didn't need to" = not necessary, so we didn't.

questions.sentence: They ___ have warned us about the sale. We missed it!
questions.explanation: Criticism: they didn't warn us.

questions.sentence: I ___ have paid by card. It would have been easier.
questions.explanation: "Could have + past participle" for a possibility that wasn't taken.

questions.sentence: You ___ to come with me, but I'm glad you did.
questions.explanation: "Didn't have to" here focuses on lack of obligation.

questions.sentence: ___ I need is a holiday.
questions.explanation: "What + clause + is..." is a cleft sentence used to add emphasis.

questions.sentence: It was the salary ___ attracted me to the job.
questions.explanation: "It was ... that..." emphasises one part of the sentence.

questions.sentence: I ___ like the job, but the hours are too long.
questions.explanation: Use "do/does/did" before the main verb for emphasis.

questions.sentence: She ___ work hard last year. She deserved the promotion.
questions.explanation: "Did + base form" for emphasis in the past.

questions.sentence: What I love about this job ___ the people.
questions.explanation: In "What I love... is...", use "is" to connect the parts.

questions.sentence: ___ was the CEO who made the final decision.
questions.explanation: "It was + person + who..." emphasises the person.

questions.sentence: The thing ___ annoys me most is the commute.
questions.explanation: "The thing that..." is another way to add emphasis.

questions.sentence: Never ___ such a difficult interview.
questions.explanation: After negative adverbs at the start (Never), invert the subject and auxiliary.

questions.sentence: Not only ___ late, but he also forgot his CV.
questions.explanation: "Not only" at the start of a sentence requires inversion.

questions.sentence: All I want ___ a job I enjoy.
questions.explanation: "All I want is..." is an emphatic structure.

questions.sentence: Rarely ___ such a talented candidate.
questions.explanation: "Rarely" at the start requires inversion.

questions.sentence: It's not the money ___ matters, it's job satisfaction.
questions.explanation: "It's not X that..." emphasises the contrast.

questions.sentence: What happened ___ that the company closed down.
questions.explanation: "What happened was (that)..." emphasises an event.

questions.sentence: The reason ___ I left was the lack of opportunities.
questions.explanation: "The reason why... was..." is a cleft structure.

questions.sentence: Under no circumstances ___ share your password.
questions.explanation: "Under no circumstances" at the start requires inversion.

questions.sentence: Hardly ___ started when the fire alarm went off.
questions.explanation: "Hardly... when" with inversion in the past perfect.

questions.sentence: I ___ apologise for the delay.
questions.explanation: "I do apologise" is an emphatic, polite apology.

questions.sentence: It was in 2015 ___ she started her own business.
questions.explanation: "It was + time + that..." emphasises the time.

questions.sentence: What she did ___ resign immediately.
questions.explanation: "What she did was (to) + base form" emphasises an action.

questions.sentence: Little ___ that he would become the CEO one day.
questions.explanation: "Little" at the start (= not at all) requires inversion.

questions.sentence: Only after the interview ___ how nervous I had been.
questions.explanation: "Only after..." at the start requires inversion in the main clause.
